newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: VW seeks to tap emotions of potential buyers.
newsitem.headline: VW seeks to tap emotions of potential buyers.

text.p: Walk around the German carmaker stands at the Geneva car show and the catch phrase is simple -- sell cars with more emotion.
Porsche AG and Daimler-Benz AG certainly do it. BMW AG and Audi have also cultivated strong emotional bonds with their customers.
Now Volkswagen AG, Europe's largest carmaker, thinks it's time for emotions to play a greater role in its efforts to sell mass-volume vehicles.
The Wolfsburg-based carmaker hopes to grab the emotional attention of potential buyers with a successor to the Beetle, the odd-shaped car which put Volkswagen on the map in the 1960s.
VW intends to show the new Beetle, which will be built in Mexico, at the Frankfurt car show in September before its planned introduction in 1998.

"Everyone has had some sort of a relationship with the Beetle, whether it was as a small child riding in the back seat or going off to university," Robert Buechelhofer, who heads VW's sales and marketing, told Reuters in an interview.
But some industry executives believe volume car sellers cannot build emotional ties with customers, saying it should be left to pricy players such as Porsche and Daimler-Benz with the Mercedes.
Buechelhofer, a former BMW official, doesn't buy that idea.

"I cannot accept that someone would tell me that we are prohibited from entering the emotional part of the business. The world is changing and we have to definitely change along with the times," he said. "There can indeed be a lot of dynamism in this business."
Seeking to sell a car on an emotional feeling is not something new for manufacturers who have long sought to build brand images.
But the rhetoric has now been taken up a notch, in part due to intensifying competition among European car manufacturers at a time of industry saturation and fights for potential buyers.

Executives at the Geneva car show said that attracting customers merely based on price and performance or resale value would not boost a manufacturer's market share. This is driving the push to find fresh ways to differentiate vehicles.

Daimler-Benz chief executive Juergen Schrempp said at the unveiling of the Mercedes A class car, a foray into the vicious small vehicle market, that the new vehicle "speaks to the emotions and aesthetic sensibilities -- it has charm and personality all its own".
Mercedes has long sold its cars on three other key notions -- comfort, quality and safety.
Porsche has long been the best at selling cars based on emotion, with some Porsche officials saying about a quarter of its value can be attributed to the visceral grip of the car.

The Stuttgart-based carmaker has 120,000 members in Porsche clubs. It sells about 150 million marks ($88 million) a year in accessories with the Porsche brand name to people, many of whom can only dream of buying one of the cars.
"Our soul lies in the niche market," said Porsche chief executive Wendelin Wiedeking at the car show.
But Buechelhofer says VW can succeed at selling cars by creating an emotional bond with customers as well as driving home the message that VW cars are good quality for the price.
"We are going to lift the image gradually, not from today to tomorrow but step by step," he said.
He noted the success since late last year of the revamped Passat saloon, whose predecessors were long seen as mediocre vehicles but a good buy for the money.

"There were people who said we should drop the Passat name. My argument was that if we put a new content in the bottle, we can easily survive with the Passat name. My very strong feeling is after half a year that we are on track," he said.
